claims.source: Oscillatory activity in the theta range (4–8 Hz) appears to organize local neuronal ensembles across distant regions during WM processes (Buzsáki, 1996; Sarnthein et al., 1998; Rutishauser et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on theta oscillations and working memory.

claims.claim: Theta power increases during complex manipulations of items in WM.
claims.source: Theta power increases during complex manipulations of items in WM (Sauseng et al., 2005), with increasing memory load (Jensen and Tesche, 2002; Payne and Kounios, 2009), and is correlated with WM performance (Jacobs et al., 2006; Fuentemilla et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous empirical studies.

claims.claim: The relative phases of theta oscillations influence encoding and retrieval success.
claims.source: Moreover, the relative phases of these oscillations influence encoding and retrieval success (Rizzuto et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Frontoparietal theta synchrony with ~0° phase lag is associated with the maintenance and manipulation of information in WM.
claims.source: For example, frontoparietal theta synchrony with ~0° phase lag is associated with the maintenance and manipulation of information in WM (Sauseng et al., 2005; Polanía et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: In- and anti-phase theta frequency (6 Hz) stimulation was applied across two key nodes of the right frontoparietal network: the middle frontal gyrus and inferior parietal lobule.
claims.source: In- and anti-phase theta frequency (6 Hz) stimulation was applied across two key nodes of the right frontoparietal network: the middle frontal gyrus and inferior parietal lobule.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claims.claim: Similar tACS stimulation has previously been shown to produce phase-dependent modulations of WM performance.
claims.source: Similar tACS stimulation has previously been shown to produce phase-dependent modulations of WM performance (Polanía et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Increasing demand in verbal N-back conditions was associated with stronger activity and effective connectivity within the right hemisphere WM network.
claims.source: The right hemisphere was stimulated because increasing demand in verbal N-back conditions was associated with stronger activity and effective connectivity within the right hemisphere WM network (Fedorenko et al., 2013; Dima et al., 2014), as well as a more pronounced effect of tACS on WM performance (Jaušovec et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: tACS has a more pronounced effect on WM performance in the right hemisphere.
claims.source: The right hemisphere was stimulated because increasing demand in verbal N-back conditions was associated with stronger activity and effective connectivity within the right hemisphere WM network (Fedorenko et al., 2013; Dima et al., 2014), as well as a more pronounced effect of tACS on WM performance (Jaušovec et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Short trains of tACS avoid aftereffects of the stimulation whilst maximizing power to detect changes in the BOLD signal.
claims.source: Our fMRI-tACS experimental design used short trains of tACS that avoid aftereffects of the stimulation (Vossen et al., 2015) whilst maximizing power to detect changes in the blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) signal.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research and describes the methodological rationale.

claims.claim: BOLD provides a measurement of brain activity during tACS without complex artifacts that can severely contaminate traditional EEG and MEG recordings.
claims.source: Functional (f) MRI is well suited to this purpose because BOLD: (1) provides a measurement of brain activity during tACS without complex artifacts that can severely contaminate traditional electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) recordings (Cabral-Calderin et al., 2016; Vosskuhl et al., 2016; Noury et al., 2016);
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on fMRI-tACS methodology.

claims.claim: BOLD is unaffected by the phase of the applied stimulation.
claims.source: and (2) is unaffected by the phase of the applied stimulation.
claims.evidence: This is presented as an established property of BOLD imaging in the context of tACS.

claims.claim: Synchronous (in-phase) stimulation caused an improvement in performance and led to increased frontoparietal activity when cognitive demands were high.
claims.source: We found that synchronous (in-phase) stimulation caused an improvement in performance and led to increased frontoparietal activity when cognitive demands were high.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from both behavioral and fMRI measurements.

claims.claim: External manipulations of large-scale brain synchronization can be used to shape activity and connectivity within brain networks, and those modulations are detectable using fMRI.
claims.source: These results show that external manipulations of large-scale brain synchronization can be used to shape activity and connectivity within brain networks, and those modulations are detectable using fMRI.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claims.claim: Underlying cognitive demand has an important influence on the neural effects of tACS.
claims.source: We additionally demonstrate the important influence of underlying cognitive demand on the neural effects of tACS.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing differential effects across task conditions.

claims.claim: Ten healthy volunteers performed a session of each tACS condition (synchronous, desynchronous and sham) in a pseudo-randomized single-blinded cross-over design.
claims.source: Ten healthy volunteers performed a session of each tACS condition (synchronous, desynchronous and sham) in a pseudo-randomized single-blinded cross-over design.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design of Experiment 1.

claims.claim: There was a significant main effect of task on reaction time in Experiment 1.
claims.source: For RTs, there was a significant main effect of task (F(2,18)=45.47, p<0.001, ηp2=0.84), tACS condition (F(2,18)=8.02, p=0.003, ηp2=0.47) and task x tACS condition interaction (F(4,36)=3.20, p=0.024, ηp2=0.26).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claims.claim: There was a significant main effect of tACS condition on reaction time in Experiment 1.
claims.source: For RTs, there was a significant main effect of task (F(2,18)=45.47, p<0.001, ηp2=0.84), tACS condition (F(2,18)=8.02, p=0.003, ηp2=0.47) and task x tACS condition interaction (F(4,36)=3.20, p=0.024, ηp2=0.26).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claims.claim: There was a significant task x tACS condition interaction on reaction time in Experiment 1.
claims.source: For RTs, there was a significant main effect of task (F(2,18)=45.47, p<0.001, ηp2=0.84), tACS condition (F(2,18)=8.02, p=0.003, ηp2=0.47) and task x tACS condition interaction (F(4,36)=3.20, p=0.024, ηp2=0.26).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claims.claim: Synchronous stimulation improved performance on the cognitively demanding 2-back task.
claims.source: Synchronous stimulation improved performance on the cognitively demanding 2-back task. A main effect of tACS condition on RTs was observed (F(2,18)=7.65, p=0.004, ηp2=0.46).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claims.claim: Synchronous tACS resulted in faster responses compared to desynchronous tACS in the 2-back task.
claims.source: This reflected faster responses in the synchronous compared to both the desynchronous (t(9) = −5.72, p<0.001, d = 0.76) and sham conditions (t(9) = −2.43, p=0.038, d = 0.58) (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data and shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Synchronous tACS resulted in faster responses compared to sham in the 2-back task.
claims.source: This reflected faster responses in the synchronous compared to both the desynchronous (t(9) = −5.72, p<0.001, d = 0.76) and sham conditions (t(9) = −2.43, p=0.038, d = 0.58) (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data and shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: There was no difference between the RTs in the desynchronous and sham conditions for the 2-back task.
claims.source: In contrast, there was no difference between the RTs in the desynchronous and sham conditions (t(9) = 0.76, p=0.468, d = 0.15).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claims.claim: There was no effect of stimulation on RTs for the less demanding 1-back condition.
claims.source: There was no effect of stimulation on RTs for the less demanding 1-back (F(2,18)=1.11, p=0.351, ηp2=0.11) and CRT (F(2,18)=1.50, p=0.251, ηp2=0.14) conditions, supporting a role for phase synchronization during demanding WM processes and ruling out a simple motor effect.
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claims.claim: There was no effect of stimulation on RTs for the CRT condition.
claims.source: There was no effect of stimulation on RTs for the less demanding 1-back (F(2,18)=1.11, p=0.351, ηp2=0.11) and CRT (F(2,18)=1.50, p=0.251, ηp2=0.14) conditions, supporting a role for phase synchronization during demanding WM processes and ruling out a simple motor effect.
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claims.claim: The absence of tACS effects on less demanding tasks supports a role for phase synchronization during demanding WM processes and rules out a simple motor effect.
claims.source: There was no effect of stimulation on RTs for the less demanding 1-back (F(2,18)=1.11, p=0.351, ηp2=0.11) and CRT (F(2,18)=1.50, p=0.251, ηp2=0.14) conditions, supporting a role for phase synchronization during demanding WM processes and ruling out a simple motor effect.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of behavioral results.

claims.claim: The expected slowing of RTs was observed for 2-back relative to 1-back performance in desynchronous and sham conditions.
claims.source: While the expected slowing of RTs was observed for 2-back relative to 1-back performance in desynchronous and sham conditions (paired t-test between 1-back and 2-back: desynchronous tACS: t(9) = −4.19, p=0.002; sham: t(9) = −3.41, p=0.008), there was no significant difference in performance when the synchronous stimulation was applied (t(9) = −1.88, p=0.093).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference in performance between 2-back and 1-back when synchronous stimulation was applied.
claims.source: While the expected slowing of RTs was observed for 2-back relative to 1-back performance in desynchronous and sham conditions (paired t-test between 1-back and 2-back: desynchronous tACS: t(9) = −4.19, p=0.002; sham: t(9) = −3.41, p=0.008), there was no significant difference in performance when the synchronous stimulation was applied (t(9) = −1.88, p=0.093).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claims.claim: Accuracy was unaffected by stimulation in Experiment 1.
claims.source: Accuracy was unaffected by stimulation, as no main effect of tACS condition (F(2,18)=1.01, p=0.383, ηp2=0.10) or task x tACS condition interaction (F(4,36)=0.51, p=0.730, ηp2=0.05) was observed.
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claims.claim: There was a main effect of task condition on accuracy in Experiment 1.
claims.source: As expected, the repeated-measures ANOVA resulted in a main effect of task condition (F(2,18)=15.20, p<0.001, ηp2=0.63), with the 2-back condition showing lower accuracy than the 1-back and CRT conditions (2-back: 83.9% ± 3.7%; 1-back: 95.6% ± 1.5%; CRT: 96.3% ± 0.7%).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claims.claim: The 2-back condition showed lower accuracy than the 1-back and CRT conditions.
claims.source: As expected, the repeated-measures ANOVA resulted in a main effect of task condition (F(2,18)=15.20, p<0.001, ηp2=0.63), with the 2-back condition showing lower accuracy than the 1-back and CRT conditions (2-back: 83.9% ± 3.7%; 1-back: 95.6% ± 1.5%; CRT: 96.3% ± 0.7%).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claims.claim: Twenty-four participants underwent a session of simultaneous tACS-fMRI in Experiment 2.
claims.source: Twenty-four participants underwent a session of simultaneous tACS-fMRI (Figure 2A) in which they performed separate runs of blocked 2-back and CRT tasks, for both the synchronous (0° relative phase) and desynchronous (180° relative phase) tACS conditions (N = 21 for 2-back task and N = 20 for CRT task, see Materials and methods for exclusion criteria).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design of Experiment 2.

claims.claim: TACS stimulation did not significantly impact behavior across stimulation conditions in Experiment 2.
claims.source: TACS stimulation did not significantly impact behavior across stimulation conditions, consistent with its use as a physiological probe (Driver et al., 2009; Fedorenko et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data and citations to similar methodological approaches.

claims.claim: There was no significant main effect of tACS condition on RTs or accuracy in Experiment 2.
claims.source: There was no significant main effect of tACS condition on RTs or accuracy, or interaction between task (2-back and CRT) and tACS condition (all F values < 1, all p values > 0.4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claims.claim: There was a main effect of task on RTs in Experiment 2.
claims.source: As expected, there was a main effect of task on RTs (F(1,18)=73.16, p<0.001, ηp2=0.80) and accuracy (F(1,18)=81.68, p<0.001, ηp2=0.82), driven by slower responses (2-back: 0.66 ± 0.24 s; CRT: 0.44 ± 0.1 s) and reduced accuracy (2-back: 80.2% ± 1.7%; CRT: 97.1% ± 0.8%) in the 2-back than in the CRT task conditions, attributable to the expected differences in task difficulty.
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claims.claim: There was a main effect of task on accuracy in Experiment 2.
claims.source: As expected, there was a main effect of task on RTs (F(1,18)=73.16, p<0.001, ηp2=0.80) and accuracy (F(1,18)=81.68, p<0.001, ηp2=0.82), driven by slower responses (2-back: 0.66 ± 0.24 s; CRT: 0.44 ± 0.1 s) and reduced accuracy (2-back: 80.2% ± 1.7%; CRT: 97.1% ± 0.8%) in the 2-back than in the CRT task conditions, attributable to the expected differences in task difficulty.
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claims.claim: 2-back performance was associated with increased BOLD signal in visual cortex, caudate, thalamus, cerebellum, lateral premotor cortex, dorsal cingulate and medial premotor cortex, dorsolateral and ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, frontal poles and medial and lateral posterior parietal cortex.
claims.source: 2-back performance was associated with increased BOLD signal in visual cortex, caudate, thalamus, cerebellum, lateral premotor cortex, dorsal cingulate and medial premotor cortex, dorsolateral and ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, frontal poles and medial and lateral posterior parietal cortex (Figure 3A, left).
claims.evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: CRT performance was associated with increased activity within bilateral sensory motor regions, as well as in the supplementary motor area, visual cortex, thalamus and the putamen.
claims.source: CRT performance was associated with increased activity within bilateral sensory motor regions, as well as in the supplementary motor area, visual cortex, thalamus and the putamen (Figure 3A, right).
claims.evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The activity in the frontoparietal networks was higher for the 2-back than for the CRT task.
claims.source: As expected, the activity in the frontoparietal networks was higher for the 2-back than for the CRT task.
claims.evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis.

claims.claim: Deactivation of the default mode network (DMN) regions was observed for both the CRT and 2-back tasks compared to rest.
claims.source: Deactivation of the default mode network (DMN) regions was observed for both the CRT and 2-back tasks compared to rest, with extensive deactivation in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and frontal orbital cortex seen during 2-back performance (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Task-related BOLD responses were increased in the IPL and MFG regions for the synchronous tACS condition selectively during performance of the 2-back task.
claims.source: Task-related BOLD responses were increased in the IPL and MFG regions for the synchronous tACS condition (tACS 0° > tACS OFF) selectively during performance of the 2-back task (Figure 3B), but not during the desynchronous tACS condition (tACS 180° > tACS OFF).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ROI analysis of fMRI data and shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: A negative correlation was observed between participants' mean BOLD signal in the IPL-electrode region and their mean RTs during synchronous tACS.
claims.source: A negative correlation was observed between participants' mean BOLD signal in the IPL-electrode region and their mean RTs during synchronous tACS (r(21)= −0.39, p=0.039, one-tailed), indicating that across participants increased brain activity related to reduced RTs (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of fMRI and behavioral data and shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: No correlation was observed between BOLD signal in the MFG-electrode region and RTs during synchronous tACS.
claims.source: No correlation was observed for the MFG-electrode region (r(21)= −0.29, p=0.103, one-tailed).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of fMRI and behavioral data.

claims.claim: During performance of the CRT task, the BOLD response was increased only for the synchronous tACS condition and exclusively in the MFG-electrode region.
claims.source: During performance of the CRT task, the BOLD response was increased only for the synchronous tACS condition (tACS 0° > tACS OFF) and exclusively in the MFG-electrode region (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ROI analysis of fMRI data and shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: No correlation was observed between the increased BOLD response in the MFG and RTs during synchronous tACS in the CRT task.
claims.source: No correlation was observed between the increased BOLD response in the MFG and RTs during synchronous tACS.
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of fMRI and behavioral data.

claims.claim: There was no difference in BOLD signal in the return electrode region (T8) in any of the tACS or task conditions.
claims.source: Furthermore, to test whether the measured effects of tACS on brain activity could be explained by a simple direct effect of the electric current on the BOLD signal, we investigated activity in the brain region corresponding to the return electrode (electrode at T8, over the right middle temporal gyrus, Figure 1A). There was no difference in BOLD signal for this region in any of the tACS or task conditions.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ROI analysis of fMRI data.

claims.claim: During fixation periods with tACS stimulation, neither the synchronous nor the desynchronous tACS conditions elicited differences in BOLD signal compared to baseline.
claims.source: Similarly, during fixation periods with tACS stimulation, neither the synchronous nor the desynchronous tACS conditions elicited differences in BOLD signal compared to baseline (fixation periods without stimulation), for either the 2-back or the CRT tasks.
claims.evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis.

claims.claim: Synchronous tACS applied during performance of the 2-back task increased neural activity in the right frontoparietal network.
claims.source: Synchronous tACS applied during performance of the 2-back task had a widespread effect on regions normally activated by task performance (tACS 0° > tACS OFF). Neural activity increased in the right frontoparietal network, with peaks of increased BOLD activity seen in the right lateral prefrontal cortex, middle frontal gyrus and bilaterally in the posterior parietal cortices
claims.evidence: This is supported by whole-brain fMRI data analysis.

claims.claim: Synchronous tACS during the 2-back task increased BOLD activity bilaterally in the thalamus, basal ganglia, occipital cortex and inferior temporal gyrus.
claims.source: Additionally, BOLD activity increases were seen bilaterally in the thalamus, basal ganglia, occipital cortex and inferior temporal gyrus (Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1, table supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by whole-brain fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Desynchronous tACS during the 2-back task increased deactivation in parts of the default mode network.
claims.source: A distinct pattern was observed for the desynchronous tACS condition. Increased deactivation (tACS 180° < tACS OFF) was observed in parts of the default mode network (DMN), namely the posterior cingulate cortex, precuneus, ventromedial PFC, left orbitofrontal cortex and left parahippocampal gyrus (Figure 4B and Supplementary file 1, table supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by whole-brain fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Direct contrast of synchronous and desynchronous stimulation revealed differences in the left hemisphere inferior parietal lobule (IPL), superior frontal gyrus (SFG) and orbitofrontal cortex (OFC).
claims.source: We directly contrasted synchronous and desynchronous stimulation using the contrast (tACS 0° > tACS OFF) > (tACS 180° > tACS OFF). This revealed differences induced by the two tACS phase conditions in the left hemisphere inferior parietal lobule (IPL), superior frontal gyrus (SFG) and orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), Figure 4C, explained by increased deactivation for the desynchronous compared to the synchronous tACS condition (Figure 4C and Supplementary file 1, table supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by whole-brain fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The less demanding CRT task resulted in similar increases in BOLD activity in the occipital cortex for both synchronous and desynchronous tACS.
claims.source: The less demanding CRT task resulted in similar increases in BOLD activity in the occipital cortex for both synchronous and desynchronous tACS.
claims.evidence: This is supported by whole-brain fMRI data analysis.

claims.claim: Desynchronous tACS during the CRT task increased BOLD signal in the supplementary motor cortex.
claims.source: Additionally, increased BOLD signal was observed for the supplementary motor cortex during the desynchronous tACS condition and right frontal orbital/insular cortex for the synchronous condition (Figure 4B and Supplementary file 1, tables supplement 4 and 5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by whole-brain fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Synchronous tACS during the CRT task increased BOLD signal in the right frontal orbital/insular cortex.
claims.source: Additionally, increased BOLD signal was observed for the supplementary motor cortex during the desynchronous tACS condition and right frontal orbital/insular cortex for the synchronous condition (Figure 4B and Supplementary file 1, tables supplement 4 and 5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by whole-brain fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: No differences in the contrasts for synchronous vs desynchronous stimulation were observed for the CRT task.
claims.source: No differences in the contrasts for synchronous vs desynchronous stimulation were observed for the CRT task.
claims.evidence: This is supported by whole-brain fMRI data analysis.

claims.claim: Externally inducing synchronization or desynchronization of the right frontoparietal network modulates activity across large-scale networks in a cognitive state dependent manner.
claims.source: These results show that externally inducing synchronization or desynchronization of the right frontoparietal network modulates activity across large-scale networks in a cognitive state dependent manner, such that phase dependent effects were observed clearly for the 2-back task, when cognitive demands were high.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pattern of fMRI results across different task conditions.

claims.claim: During fixation periods with simultaneous tACS stimulation, no increases in the BOLD signal compared to baseline were observed.
claims.source: This was further confirmed during fixation periods with simultaneous tACS stimulation. For this condition, we observed no increases in the BOLD signal compared to baseline (fixation periods without tACS).
claims.evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis.

claims.claim: Increased deactivation was observed during fixation with tACS in a number of brain regions, but there were no phase dependent differences during the CRT or 2-back runs.
claims.source: Increased deactivation was observed in a number of brain regions, but there were no phase dependent differences during the CRT or 2-back runs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Synchronous tACS during the 2-back task increased FC between the right IPL and posterior parts of the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC).
claims.source: Synchronous tACS during the 2-back task increased FC between the right IPL and posterior parts of the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) (Figure 5 and Supplementary file 1, table supplement 6) compared to the FC observed during task performance in the absence of stimulation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by PPI analysis of fMRI data and shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: No modulation of FC was observed for the MFG-electrode seed during synchronous tACS in the 2-back task.
claims.source: In contrast, no modulation of FC was observed for the MFG-electrode seed.
claims.evidence: This is supported by PPI analysis of fMRI data.

claims.claim: Desynchronous tACS produced increases in FC in occipito/temporal regions in a similar pattern for both MFG- and IPL-electrode seeds.
claims.source: Desynchronous tACS produced increases in FC in occipito/temporal regions in a similar pattern for both MFG- and IPL-electrode seeds (Figure 5 and Supplementary file 1, table supplement 6).
claims.evidence: This is supported by PPI analysis of fMRI data and shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: There was no correlation between FC in the 2-back task and RTs.
claims.source: There was no correlation between FC in the 2-back task and RTs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of functional connectivity and behavioral data.

claims.claim: The tACS phase dependent modulation of FC observed for the 2-back task was absent for the CRT task.
claims.source: The tACS phase dependent modulation of FC observed for the 2-back task was absent for the CRT task, where no modulations of FC were observed.
claims.evidence: This is supported by PPI analysis of fMRI data.

claims.claim: Functional connectivity using the return electrode region as seed did not show any modulations in FC in either the 2-back or CRT tasks.
claims.source: As a control, we also investigated functional connectivity using the return electrode region as seed, which did not show any modulations in FC in either the 2-back or CRT tasks.
claims.evidence: This is supported by PPI analysis of fMRI data.

claims.claim: No modulation of FC was observed during fixation periods using any of the seed regions for any tACS or task conditions.
claims.source: Furthermore, no modulation of FC was observed during fixation periods using any of the seed regions for any tACS or task conditions.
claims.evidence: This is supported by PPI analysis of fMRI data.

claims.claim: There was very low movement in the fMRI sample.
claims.source: Overall, there was very low movement in our sample (mean framewise displacement (FD) for 2-back = 0.044 ± 0.013, n = 21, and CRT = 0.040 ± 0.011, n = 20)
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of motion parameters from fMRI data.

claims.claim: There was no difference in framewise displacement between periods with and without stimulation or for different tACS phase conditions for any of the tasks.
claims.source: and there was no difference in FD between periods with and without stimulation or for different tACS phase conditions for any of the tasks (Repeated measures ANOVA for CRT and 2-back with factors stimulation (ON, OFF) and tACS phase (0°, 180°); all F values < 2, all p values > 0.2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of motion parameters.

claims.claim: Heart rate was not different between periods with and without stimulation or between different tACS phase conditions.
claims.source: Similarly, heart rate (available for a subset of participants; N = 6) was not different between periods with and without stimulation or between different tACS phase conditions (Repeated measures ANOVA for CRT and 2-back with factors stimulation (ON, OFF) and tACS phase (0°, 180°); all F values < 2, all p values > 0.4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of physiological monitoring data.

claims.claim: Participants were unaware whether or not they were receiving stimulation and could not distinguish between the type of stimulation.
claims.source: In addition, analysis of post-experiment questionnaires showed that participants were unaware whether or not they were receiving stimulation and could not distinguish between the type of stimulation (Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of questionnaire data.

claims.claim: External manipulations of oscillatory synchrony across a right-sided frontoparietal network impact neural activity and modify behavior.
claims.source: Our results demonstrate that external manipulations of oscillatory synchrony across a right-sided frontoparietal network impact neural activity and modify behavior.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claims.claim: The effects of tACS depend on the relative phase of the external oscillators and also the underlying cognitive state at the time tACS is applied.
claims.source: The effects depend on the relative phase of the external oscillators and also the underlying cognitive state at the time tACS is applied.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental results showing differential effects across phase and task conditions.

claims.claim: Imposing theta frequency synchronously across the inferior parietal lobe and middle frontal gyrus improves verbal WM performance and increases frontal and parietal brain activity.
claims.source: In particular, we showed that imposing theta frequency synchronously across the inferior parietal lobe and middle frontal gyrus improves verbal WM performance and increases frontal and parietal brain activity.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the behavioral and fMRI results.

claims.claim: The functional connectivity of the inferior parietal lobe was modulated by tACS in a phase dependent manner.
claims.source: The functional connectivity of the inferior parietal lobe was also modulated by tACS in a phase dependent manner.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the functional connectivity results.

claims.claim: Frontal interactions increased with synchronous theta stimulation whereas posterior interactions increased with desynchronous stimulation.
claims.source: Frontal interactions increased with synchronous theta stimulation whereas posterior interactions increased with desynchronous stimulation, suggesting that information flow through brain regions involved in WM can be differentially affected by varying the phase of external stimulation.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the functional connectivity results.

claims.claim: Information flow through brain regions involved in WM can be differentially affected by varying the phase of external stimulation.
claims.source: Frontal interactions increased with synchronous theta stimulation whereas posterior interactions increased with desynchronous stimulation, suggesting that information flow through brain regions involved in WM can be differentially affected by varying the phase of external stimulation.

results.result: In Experiment 1, synchronous theta tACS (0° phase) applied to the right frontoparietal network improved reaction times specifically on the cognitively demanding 2-back working memory task compared to both desynchronous (180° phase) and sham stimulation, but had no effect on less demanding 1-back or choice reaction time tasks. Accuracy was unaffected by stimulation across all conditions.
results.evaluation: The behavioral results from Experiment 1 are well-supported by appropriate statistical analyses (repeated-measures ANOVA with significant main effects and interactions, followed by post-hoc t-tests with effect sizes). The task-specificity of the effect (present only for 2-back, not 1-back or CRT) strengthens the interpretation that synchronous tACS specifically enhances demanding WM processes. The sample size (n=10) is modest but consistent with prior tACS studies, and the cross-over design controls for individual differences.

results.result: In Experiment 2, simultaneous tACS-fMRI revealed that both 2-back and CRT tasks activated expected brain networks (frontoparietal for 2-back, sensorimotor for CRT), with higher frontoparietal activity for the more demanding 2-back task. However, tACS did not significantly modulate behavior in this experiment, consistent with its use as a physiological probe rather than a behavioral intervention.
results.evaluation: The fMRI activation patterns are well-characterized and consistent with established literature on working memory networks. The lack of behavioral effects in Experiment 2 is appropriately acknowledged and justified by the different experimental design (short trains vs. continuous stimulation). The statistical analyses are appropriate (repeated-measures ANOVA, n=19-21 after exclusions), and the task validation confirms differential cognitive demands.

results.result: ROI analysis of brain regions under the tACS electrodes showed that synchronous tACS selectively increased BOLD activity in both the inferior parietal lobule (IPL) and middle frontal gyrus (MFG) during the 2-back task, but not during desynchronous stimulation. Increased IPL activity correlated negatively with reaction times (r=-0.39, p=0.039), linking neural modulation to behavioral performance. During the CRT task, only the MFG showed increased activity with synchronous tACS, without behavioral correlation.
results.evaluation: The ROI analyses are well-designed with appropriate controls (return electrode region, fixation periods) showing no effects, ruling out simple current-induced BOLD artifacts. The brain-behavior correlation for IPL is statistically significant and theoretically meaningful, though the correlation for MFG was not significant. The task-specificity of effects (different patterns for 2-back vs. CRT) supports state-dependent modulation. However, the correlation is modest (r=-0.39) and based on one-tailed testing, which should be interpreted cautiously.

results.result: Whole-brain analysis revealed that synchronous tACS during the 2-back task increased activity across widespread networks including the right frontoparietal network, thalamus, basal ganglia, and visual cortex, while desynchronous tACS increased deactivation in default mode network regions. These phase-dependent effects were specific to the cognitively demanding 2-back task; the CRT task showed similar occipital activation for both tACS phases without phase-dependent differences. No phase-dependent effects were observed during fixation periods.
results.evaluation: The whole-brain analyses use appropriate statistical thresholding (cluster-corrected Z>2.3, p<0.05 FWE) and reveal theoretically coherent patterns: synchronous tACS enhances task-positive networks while desynchronous tACS affects task-negative (DMN) regions. The cognitive state-dependency is convincingly demonstrated by the contrast between 2-back and CRT tasks, and the absence of effects during fixation provides important control evidence. The widespread effects beyond stimulation sites suggest network-level modulation rather than simple local effects.

results.result: Functional connectivity analysis using psychophysiological interaction (PPI) showed that synchronous tACS during the 2-back task increased connectivity between the right IPL and left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), while desynchronous tACS increased connectivity between both IPL and MFG seeds with occipito-temporal regions. These phase-dependent connectivity modulations were specific to the 2-back task and absent during the CRT task, fixation periods, and when using the return electrode as a control seed.
results.evaluation: The PPI analyses appropriately test for task-dependent changes in functional connectivity and include multiple important controls (CRT task, fixation periods, return electrode seed) that all show null results, strengthening the specificity of the findings. The asymmetry in connectivity effects (IPL but not MFG showing frontoparietal connectivity increases) is acknowledged and discussed. However, the lack of brain-behavior correlation for connectivity measures (C69) limits the functional interpretation of these network changes.

results.result: Control analyses confirmed that the observed tACS effects were not confounded by motion artifacts, physiological changes, or participant awareness. Framewise displacement was very low and did not differ between stimulation conditions. Heart rate (measured in a subset of participants) showed no differences across conditions. Participants were unable to reliably detect whether they were receiving stimulation or distinguish between stimulation types.
results.evaluation: The control analyses address important potential confounds. Motion analysis is thorough with appropriate statistics showing no differences across conditions. The heart rate analysis is limited by small sample size (n=6) but shows consistent null results. The blinding assessment demonstrates that participants could not distinguish conditions, ruling out expectancy effects. These controls strengthen confidence in the specificity of the tACS effects, though the heart rate data would benefit from a larger sample.

results.result: The study demonstrates that external manipulation of oscillatory synchrony across the right frontoparietal network causally impacts neural activity and behavior in a phase-dependent and cognitive state-dependent manner. Synchronous theta tACS improves working memory performance and increases frontoparietal activity and connectivity specifically when cognitive demands are high, with the behavioral improvement sufficient to eliminate the typical performance difference between 2-back and 1-back tasks.
results.evaluation: This overarching conclusion is well-supported by the convergent evidence from behavioral (Experiment 1), brain activity (Experiment 2 ROI and whole-brain analyses), and connectivity (PPI) results. The phase-dependency is demonstrated by differential effects of synchronous vs. desynchronous stimulation, and state-dependency by the specificity to high-demand (2-back) vs. low-demand (1-back, CRT) tasks. The causal claim is justified by the experimental manipulation. However, the mechanistic interpretation regarding 'oscillatory synchrony' is somewhat indirect since the study cannot directly measure oscillatory changes with fMRI (acknowledged in C135).

results.result: The neuroimaging results reveal the neural mechanisms underlying tACS-induced cognitive enhancement: synchronous stimulation increases activity in the inferior parietal lobule and middle frontal gyrus—key regions for working memory—with parietal activity correlating with faster responses. The effects extend beyond stimulation sites to include salience, visuospatial, and basal ganglia networks, suggesting network-level rather than purely local modulation. The pattern resembles pharmacological cognitive enhancement with methylphenidate.
results.evaluation: The interpretation is well-grounded in the fMRI data and supported by extensive citations to prior literature on the functional roles of these regions (C95-C101). The brain-behavior correlation (C98) provides important evidence linking neural changes to performance. The comparison to methylphenidate effects (C106) is interesting but speculative (C107), as it's based on a single cited study and the mechanisms may differ substantially. The claim about network-level effects (C105) is supported by the widespread activation patterns, though the specific mechanisms remain unclear.

results.result: The functional connectivity results suggest that altering phase synchrony controls information flow within working memory networks: synchronous tACS enhances frontoparietal connectivity (IPL-DLPFC) supporting high-demand processing, while desynchronous tACS shifts connectivity toward posterior (occipito-temporal) regions, potentially reflecting disruption of top-down control. This pattern is consistent with theoretical models proposing that phase relations enable selective routing of information and may involve frequency-specific directional communication channels.
results.evaluation: The connectivity findings (C66-C68) are empirically supported, but the mechanistic interpretations are largely speculative. The explanation for asymmetric connectivity effects (C113-C116) involves multiple speculative hypotheses about ceiling effects and frequency-specific directional communication. The interpretation of desynchronous effects as 'restoration of default connectivity' (C120) is speculative. While the theoretical framework is well-cited (C121-C123), the study cannot directly test these mechanisms with fMRI. The lack of brain-behavior correlations for connectivity (C69) further limits functional interpretation.

results.result: The results demonstrate that tACS effects are highly dependent on underlying brain state and network dynamics. The 2-back task, which more heavily engages the frontoparietal network than the CRT task, showed clear phase-dependent modulation of activity and connectivity, while the less demanding CRT task showed minimal phase-dependent effects. This supports theoretical predictions that entrainment is more effective when networks are actively engaged.
results.evaluation: The state-dependency is convincingly demonstrated by the systematic differences between 2-back and CRT tasks across multiple analyses (activity, connectivity). The theoretical framework is well-supported by citations (C83-C85), and the empirical results (C86-C87) directly test and confirm these predictions. The conclusion that effects cannot be predicted by current density models alone (C126, C129) is supported by the specificity of effects to task-engaged regions despite broader current distribution. This represents an important conceptual advance in understanding tACS mechanisms.

results.result: The study acknowledges several methodological limitations: unbalanced electric field distribution between tACS conditions due to the common return electrode, relatively large stimulation area potentially affecting functionally diverse subregions, and likely inter-individual variability in optimal stimulation parameters. However, the results could not be predicted by current density models alone, as effects were restricted to task-engaged regions. Future optimization may require subject-specific parameter selection using machine learning and real-time imaging.
results.evaluation: The limitations are honestly and thoroughly discussed. The electric field modeling (C124-C125, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) demonstrates the unbalanced distribution, but the control analyses (C127-C128) showing no effects at the return electrode support that results reflect network dynamics rather than simple current effects. The acknowledgment of spatial resolution limitations (C130) and individual variability (C131) is appropriate. The suggestions for future work (C132-C133) are reasonable but speculative. These limitations do not invalidate the main findings but appropriately contextualize their interpretation.

results.result: While the fMRI approach provided good spatial resolution without electrical artifacts, the study cannot specify which brain frequencies were modulated by tACS because the correspondence between brain oscillations and BOLD signal is not fully understood, and tACS might induce cross-frequency coupling.
results.evaluation: This is an honest and important limitation. The study's title and framing emphasize 'oscillatory synchronization' and 'theta frequency' effects, but the BOLD signal cannot directly measure oscillatory activity or confirm that 6 Hz stimulation specifically entrained theta oscillations. The citations (C136-C137) support that this is a known limitation of the fMRI-tACS approach. This limitation is significant for mechanistic interpretation but does not undermine the demonstration of phase-dependent and state-dependent effects on brain activity and behavior.

results.result: The findings are contextualized within the broader transcranial electrical stimulation literature, noting that tDCS also modulates working memory (with small but significant effects in meta-analyses) and can influence oscillatory activity in distant regions. However, different tES modalities impact brain excitability to different degrees, and working memory performance is sensitive to stimulation parameters, suggesting that careful consideration of target mechanisms is needed.
results.evaluation: The discussion appropriately situates the findings within the broader tES literature with relevant citations to meta-analyses (C139-C140) and mechanistic studies (C142-C145). The acknowledgment that different modalities may work through different mechanisms (C144) is important for interpretation. However, the comparison between tACS and tDCS is somewhat superficial and doesn't deeply address whether they share mechanisms. The discussion serves mainly to contextualize rather than critically evaluate the relationship between different stimulation approaches.

results.result: The work demonstrates the potential of simultaneous tACS-fMRI as a methodological approach for understanding the neural mechanisms underlying externally induced oscillatory synchronization.
results.evaluation: This methodological contribution is supported by the successful implementation of the tACS-fMRI protocol, the absence of significant artifacts (C18, C134), and the ability to detect phase-dependent and state-dependent neural effects. The approach represents a technical advance over previous methods that relied on pre/post measurements or were limited by electrical artifacts in EEG/MEG. However, the fundamental limitation regarding oscillatory measurements (C135-C137) means the method reveals effects on BOLD activity and connectivity but cannot directly confirm oscillatory entrainment.
